paper_uuid: Gary Habermas - Chapter 008 - The Evidential THRESHOLD for Resurrection Belief - Gary Habermas

stories.title_or_label: The Real Seeker Show percentage anecdote
characters_or_agents: unnamed host of the Real Seeker Show
stories.setting_or_context: A prior broadcast interview in which Habermas was asked what percentage of scholarly support he required before using a source
stories.plot_or_sequence: Habermas once gave a percentage on the Real Seeker Show; he now refuses to repeat a number because critics will treat it as a universal threshold.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: Self-deprecating, cautious; used to preempt misquotation

boundaries.what_it_shows: Habermas has previously been asked for and given a percentage, and he now avoids doing so.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: It does not establish that no evidential threshold exists, nor that his prior percentage was correct or incorrect.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: A recording showing he never gave a percentage, or that he continues to give one.

stories.notes: Anecdotal; functions as a rhetorical shield against the objection in A06.

stories.setting_or_context: Dale's former agnostic period, when he used a 51% evidential threshold
stories.plot_or_sequence: Dale used to require 51% evidence; Habermas playfully mocked him; Dale laughed graciously; Habermas now declines to name his own number.

boundaries.what_it_shows: The interviewer once held a numerical threshold and Habermas found it worth teasing.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: It does not show that numerical thresholds are irrational, only that Habermas avoids stating one.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that Dale never held a 51% threshold or that Habermas never teased him.

stories.notes: Personal banter; separable from the substantive argument.

stories.plot_or_sequence: Habermas has feet of sources and a file cabinet of papers but no numerical count except for the empty tomb.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: Defensive, earnest; appeals to labor and volume of research

boundaries.what_it_shows: Habermas possesses extensive source material and has not tabulated percentages for most facts.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: It does not show that his evidence is strong, only that it is voluminous; volume is not warrant.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Discovery that he has in fact tabulated percentages for the minimal facts.

stories.notes: Volume of sources is offered as a substitute for a numerical threshold; this is rhetorical, not evidential.

stories.title_or_label: The empty tomb head count exception
stories.setting_or_context: Habermas's own study on the empty tomb
stories.plot_or_sequence: The only time Habermas counted scholarly opinion was his own empty-tomb study, which is not one of the minimal facts; he reports roughly 80% there and 90% descriptively for the minimal facts but insists he never counted the latter.

boundaries.what_it_shows: Habermas distinguishes his one counted study from his general practice.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: It does not show that the 90% figure for the minimal facts is accurate; he explicitly disclaims having counted it.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that he has counted scholarly percentages for the minimal facts.

stories.notes: Structurally load-bearing for A02; the distinction between counted and uncounted figures is central to his reply.

stories.title_or_label: Jimmy Dunn and the early creed
stories.setting_or_context: Modern New Testament scholarship on the dating of the resurrection creed in 1 Corinthians 15
stories.plot_or_sequence: Dunn, a non-evangelical scholar, is described as open to the data and as suggesting the creedal statements may have arisen within months of the crucifixion; Ehrman concedes it is a historical fact that the disciples thought they saw the risen Jesus; Lüdemann says the preaching began immediately.

boundaries.what_it_shows: Some non-evangelical scholars affirm early testimony and the disciples' experiences.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: It does not show that the resurrection occurred; it shows only that certain scholars date the tradition early and grant the disciples' experiences.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that Dunn, Ehrman, or Lüdemann did not say these things or that their positions are misrepresented.

stories.notes: Hostile-witness testimony is used as evidence for A04; the narrative itself is separable but the cited scholars' statements are treated as data.

stories.plot_or_sequence: Critics dismiss the Gospels for reporting miracles; Habermas counters that Herodotus, Tacitus, and Suetonius also report supernatural events, so the objection is inconsistent.

boundaries.what_it_shows: Some ancient historians reported supernatural events.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: It does not show that any reported miracle occurred, nor that the Gospels' miracles are thereby credible; it only removes a consistency objection.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that these historians did not report supernatural events or that the comparison is anachronistic.

stories.notes: A tu quoque move; the historical claim is supported by A05 but the inference to Gospel credibility is not warranted by the analogy alone.

stories.setting_or_context: Discussion of the relative weight of criterion 1 versus criterion 2
stories.plot_or_sequence: Habermas says criterion 1 (high evidence) is 85-90% of the game, while criterion 2 (scholarly consensus) is far less important.

boundaries.what_it_shows: Habermas weights strong evidence far above scholarly consensus.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: It does not quantify the actual weight; the 85-90% is an informal analogy, not a measured threshold.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that Habermas treats consensus as equally or more important.

stories.notes: Ironically uses a percentage while disclaiming percentages; the analogy is explanatory, not evidential.

narrative_arc.opening_device: Interviewer asks Habermas to specify his evidential threshold, invoking a prior playful exchange about 51%.
narrative_arc.central_tension: Habermas wants to affirm strong evidence for the resurrection while refusing to name a numerical threshold, because any number will be misrepresented as a universal requirement.
narrative_arc.resolution_or_payoff: He substitutes categories (multiple attestation, eyewitness, early sources) for numbers, cites non-evangelical scholars as corroboration, and ranks criterion 1 far above criterion 2.

notes: The chapter is largely meta-methodological: it is about how Habermas frames evidence, not about new historical data. Most narrative content is anecdotal or illustrative and separable from the argument; the Dunn/Ehrman/Lüdemann and ancient-historian material is treated as evidence and is therefore less separable. No story here transfers warrant to the resurrection claim itself.
